picks.title: Stop Looking for Symbols: The Deepest Embodied & Visceral Truth of the Lulav & Esrog
picks.summary: The idea is that a Mitzvah is not merely a symbol pointing toward some deeper spiritual truth. The act itself is the encounter.We often ask, “What does the Lulav symbolize? What does the Esrog represent?” Those questions can be meaningful, but they can also subtly turn the Mitzvah into a metaphor for something else. Judaism asks us to go further: to take the Lulav, hold the Esrog, move the body, and enter the Mitzvah physically.The meaning is not only something we understand. It is something we do. picks.reason: Focuses on embodied mitzvah practice, emphasizing direct encounter over symbolic meaning.

picks.title: Succos - Yes But Do You Still Love Me? The Embrace of the Sukkah After Yom Kippur
picks.summary: If the Ananei HaKavod first surrounded the Jewish people when they left Mitzrayim, why do we celebrate Sukkos in Tishrei? The Gra explains that Sukkos commemorates the clouds that returned after the cheit ha’eigel and the forgiveness of Yom Kippur. These were not the clouds of an innocent relationship. They were the clouds that came back.Being forgiven does not always mean that we know how to feel close again. Sukkos is Hashem’s answer to that fear: Come sit with Me. picks.reason: Explores spiritual meaning of Sukkot as a response to forgiveness and relationship with God.

picks.title: A Festival About Nothing: Dr. Tsivia Frank Wygoda on Shemini Atzeret-Simhat Torah
picks.summary: In Israel, Shemini Atzeret-Simhat Torah feels like the busiest day of the year.  So many prayers; so many different atmospheres.  Year after year, juggling back and forth from the joy of celebrating the completion of the annual Torah cycle with singing, dancing, and endless Torah readings, to the more somber parts of the holiday—Yizkor; the prayer for rain—leaves me exhausted and a little dizzy, almost wishing for the peace and quiet of “aharei ha-hagim - after the holidays.”
picks.reason: Explores the complex spiritual and emotional experience of Shemini Atzeret-Simhat Torah holiday in Israel.
